questions.question: Why does char_ngrams wrap a word such as "where" in angle brackets?
options: They force every word to have exactly two characters
They turn the word into a BPE merge before counting
The boundary markers let n-grams represent the beginning and end of the word
They remove all internal character n-grams
questions.explanation: char_ngrams builds <where> first, so n-grams can encode boundary information as well as interior spelling.

questions.question: Why does char_ngrams return a set rather than a list?
options: A set preserves the exact left-to-right order of every slice
A set stores the frequency of each character automatically
The function returns only the whole word and no n-grams
Repeated slices should contribute one shared subword feature
questions.explanation: The implementation collects the wrapped word and generated slices in a set, removing duplicate strings.

questions.question: What symbol sequence does init_vocab create for the word "low"?
options: ("l", "o", "w") without a boundary symbol
questions.explanation: The BPE vocabulary starts from characters and appends the explicit end-of-word symbol </w>.

questions.question: How does learn_bpe choose the first merge?
options: It chooses the alphabetically first character pair
It selects the adjacent pair with the highest frequency weighted by each word's corpus count
It merges the longest word before counting pairs
It samples a pair uniformly from all vocabulary entries
questions.explanation: pair_freq adds each pair's word frequency and most_common(1) supplies the next merge.

questions.question: Why does apply_bpe apply the learned merges in their stored order?
options: The order only changes display formatting, never the tokenization
Applying merges backward is required to recover characters
Later merges depend on symbols created by earlier merges
It uses the word frequency to choose a new order for every input
questions.explanation: Each merge list records a sequence of vocabulary-building operations; replaying that sequence produces compatible subword pieces.

questions.question: What is the main FastText advantage for an unseen word such as "whereupon"?
options: It looks up the word in a larger word-level dictionary at inference time
It assigns the same vector to every out-of-vocabulary word
It removes morphology by mapping the word to a single [UNK] token
Known character n-grams can compose a vector even when the whole word was unseen
questions.explanation: Subword features share information across related spellings, so an OOV word can still receive a composed representation.
